item.title: The oldest rule in ZFS stopped being true, and my NAS upgrades got a lot cheaper
item.itunes:title: The oldest rule in ZFS stopped being true, and my NAS upgrades got a lot cheaper
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you start to reach a higher capacity on your NAS drive, you might start considering adding one or two more hard drives in order to gain storage, but this might break the bank.

In every ZFS forum, documentation page, and subreddit for the past two decades, the law has been seemingly absolute: you cannot expand an existing RAIDZ VDEV by adding a single disk. Instead, in order to grow your pool, you are forced into either ripping and replacing by buying six identical drives all at once and swapping them one by one over several grueling resilvered days and having to eat the cost or buying a second entire six-drive VDEV at once, demanding an expensive 12- to 24-bay chassis.

However, the release of OpenZFS RAIDZ expansion has caused a breakthrough. The stubborn inability to expand RAIDZ vdevs drove thousands of budget-conscious users into the arms of Unraid or Synology's proprietary SHR. With native OpenZFS RAIDZ expansion, you can finally buy a single hard drive on sale, slide it into an empty bay, and grow your resilient enterprise-grade pool incrementally without having to replace the entire thing.

5 open source OS options for your self-built NAS

Break free from the constraints of prebuilt NAS devices.

6
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The architecture behind RAIDZ

The problem has finally been solved

RAIDZ has been pretty inflexible for the past 20 years. This is thanks to block striping, as in traditional hardware RAID 5/6: data is striped across drives in fixed physical stripe sizes (for example, 64KB chunks). Expanding traditional RAID requires a simple mathematical restriping pass across uniform blocks.

ZFS is both a file system and a volume manager. In ZFS RAIDZ uses dynamic variable stripe widths, meaning every single file or record from 4KB up to 1MB has its own unique priority allocation calculated at the right time. This can lead to an allocation problem because every block in a RAIDZ pool has its data and parity blocks laid out explicitly across the exact number of drives present when it was written. Inserting a new drive into the middle of that geometry can break the fundamental on-disk layout assumptions.

RAIDZ expansion has solved the problem thanks to the reflow engine. The engineering behind the feature means that ZFS now performs an online reflow of the existing data. It copies and condenses existing logical stripes onto the newly widened drive geometry, creating a contiguous swath of free space at the end of every physical disk in the vdev. This means the pool stays 100% online and accessible while the expansion runs in the background too.

You could be saving thousands of dollars in the long run

Expand your storage over time

This suddenly meant that upgrading a NAS could be significantly cheaper because you could spread capital expenditure over time. Previously, you had to save up to $1,200 to drop on six drives in a single checkout session to avoid running out of capacity. However, with this new paradigm, you can buy a single 16TB or 20TB drive when it drops to an all-time low on Black Friday or Prime Day for sometimes less than $200.

Expand the array and repeat a year later, and you can slowly increase your storage so you never risk running out without footing a pricey bill. You are also no longer trapped thanks to the chassis you own. Users with standard 4-bay or 6-bay consumer enclosures are no longer locked into RAID 10 mirrors just to maintain upgrade flexibility. You can run space-efficient RAIDZ2 and still scale disk by disk.

Another benefit of expanding your storage over time is the resilver safety over time too. Instead of subjecting an aging pool to six back-to-back high-stress resilvers as you replace drives one by one, you can run a single controlled expansion pass.

There are drawbacks

Not everything is perfect

Credit: 

RAIDZ expansion is incredible and gives you the ability to expand your storage pool over time. However, it doesn't perform magic, and there are some downsides too that are worth taking note of.

The first is the priority ratio ghost space reality. The refloat process widens the physical geometry, but it does not rewrite or recalculate the data-to-parity ratio of existing blocks. This means if a file was written to a 4-wide RAIDZ2 with 50% priority overhead, it keeps that 50% ratio until it's rewritten. Only newly written files benefit from the improved priority efficiency of the wider 5-wide or 6-wide pool. This means that you might have to rebalance your files in order to actually claim 100% of your mathematical capacity from existing data. You have to rewrite the old files onto the expanded pool. You can do this using a recursive snapshot rewrite script or `zfs rebalance`.

While you do get the benefit of being able to resilver slowly, the expansion time and I/O load can be quite tough. Reflowing 40 to 80 TB of data across mechanical drives can take days or sometimes even weeks. During expansion, pool I/O performance will drop noticeably. If a drive fails during the expansion, the process pauses automatically to allow degraded pool repair/resilver before resuming.

It might be time to commit

Don't let the wall put you off

For years, enterprise ZFS storage purity came at the expense of home server practicality and thousands of dollars in your wallet. The inability to add one drive at a time was the single biggest reason DIY builders settled for proprietary solutions or compromised unstriped storage. It feels like OpenZFS has finally caught up to the economic reality of the home builder. If you've been putting off your next port expansion or hesitating to commit to ZFS because of the upgrade war, that war is officially gone.

item.title: Microsoft reveals a new Windows 11 device designed for developers, and it comes with all the basics
item.itunes:title: Microsoft reveals a new Windows 11 device designed for developers, and it comes with all the basics
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Project Zenith devices ship preconfigured for developers with dev tools and settings ready out of the box.
  • Devices can run 30B+ parameter models locally, unmetered, reducing reliance on metered cloud tokens.
  • Windows tweaks: Explorer shows hidden files/extensions, disables notifications, deepens WSL integration.

Getting a new PC is always exciting; setting it up, less so. Fortunately, if you're a developer, Microsoft is planning something big. Called "Project Zenith," it aims to give people a Windows device that comes with all the basics for programming set up out of the box, and it seems to be more than just a new variant of Windows.

Project Zenith marries hardware and software for the perfect developer experience

It's aimed at getting you up and running ASAP

As announced on the Microsoft blog, the company has announced the existence of Project Zenith. The goal behind this product is to make Windows 11 more suitable for professional, developer use, and that includes removing what its users don't need and focusing on what they do:

Project Zenith devices come with a preconfigured Windows setup for development, and a set of tools curated for what developers reach first. On these devices, developers can run 30B+ parameter models locally and unmetered – accelerating experimentation while helping reduce reliance on metered cloud tokens.

Project Zenith represents Windows at its best – listening to developers, responding with purpose and working across our ecosystem to raise the bar for what a developer PC can be.

Microsoft also notes that Project Zenith will tweak the OS to suit developers better. The File Explorer will show all the relevant data right out of the box, including hidden files and file extensions. It'll disable notifications, such as sync provider tips and account notifications. Plus, Microsoft has "integrated WSL more deeply into Windows with WSL containers" for an easier time running Linux-based apps

At first, it sounds like a new version of Windows; however, it's worth noting that Microsoft specifically mentions "Project Zenith devices." It also mentions that this version of Windows will "first become available with AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo" and will arrive on more devices down the line.

As such, this doesn't sound like a version of Windows 11 you can grab off the shelf or download from the Microsoft site; at least, not yet. It seems it'll be more like the company's previous Copilot+ devices: a range of computers designed specifically to meet a goal. The idea is that you can purchase a new Project Zenith device, boot it up, and you're already good to go. It's still early days, so we'll see what Microsoft announces further down the line.

Windows 11 finally lets you opt out of OneDrive during setup instead of just reminding you in three days

It's about time.

2
By  Simon Batt

item.title: This self-hosted tool replaced a year of backup scripts, and now I barely think about backups at all
item.itunes:title: This self-hosted tool replaced a year of backup scripts, and now I barely think about backups at all
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve learned that self-hosting comes with an unexpected problem: the more useful your server becomes, the more you have to protect it . What started as a few containers eventually turned into a setup holding files and services I actually care about. That made backup less of a side task and more of a requirement.

For a while, I handled it myself with scripts. It seemed like the obvious solution because I could control exactly what happened. But eventually, I started looking for something more reliable and easier to manage. That search led me to an open-source backup tool, Kopia, that completely changed how I handle backups.

My old backup scripts worked

But I never fully trusted them

I had a few scripts that handled different parts of my self-hosted setup. They ran on schedule, created the files I expected, and rarely caused obvious problems. The problem was the uncertainty around them. Whenever I changed something on my server, I had to wonder whether the scripts still worked the way I expected. A renamed folder, a changed Docker volume, or a small configuration change could easily make a backup incomplete without immediately being obvious.

I also found myself checking logs more often than I wanted. A successful script execution didn't always give me confidence that it had captured everything important. I was relying on the backups for files I genuinely didn't want to lose. The scripts weren't necessarily bad. I had simply outgrown them.

Kopia gave me one proper backup system

My backups finally had one home

Kopia is an open-source backup tool designed to create fast, secure, and reliable backups. It uses a repository-based approach, so instead of creating a pile of separate backup files, it stores snapshots in a structure designed for managing multiple versions of my data.

That approach immediately made more sense for my setup. I could install Kopia on my machine using Docker, create a repository, and start backing up the folders that mattered to me. I didn't have to build another collection of scripts around it. Kopia gave me a single system to work with instead of making me maintain several independent backup jobs.

I also liked that Kopia isn't tied to one type of storage. I could use local storage or send the repository somewhere else, depending on how I wanted to structure my backups. After spending so much time maintaining small scripts, having one dedicated tool handle the backup layer felt like a much cleaner approach.

Windows has too many backup tools, but this free app beats them all

I stopped trusting Windows backups after learning what actually works

1
By  Ayush Pande

The features that made me trust Kopia with my data

It handled the boring backup work

What made me trust Kopia more was how many backup tasks it handled for me. With my old scripts, I had to think about these things myself. Kopia had them built in. One of the most useful features for me is deduplication. Kopia doesn't save the same data again and again with every backup. If a file hasn't changed, it can reuse the data that is already stored. This saves space and makes it easier to keep more backup versions.

Kopia also encrypts my backups. This is important because I don't always want my backup data sitting unprotected on another storage device or server. I also liked the retention rules. Instead of manually going through old backups and deciding what to delete, I can tell Kopia how many versions I want to keep and let it handle the cleanup.

Compression helps reduce the storage space needed for the backups too. These aren't complicated features, but they removed a lot of small things I previously had to worry about. That made the whole backup process feel much more dependable.

Backing up and restoring is finally straightforward

I stopped babysitting my backups

Once I had Kopia set up, the day-to-day process became much simpler. I could schedule backups and let them run in the background instead of checking whether each individual script had done its job.

When I need to check my backups, Kopia gives me a clear view of the snapshots it has created. I can see what is available without digging through folders full of dated archives.

The restore process is just as simple. If I accidentally delete a file or need an older version, I can browse the available snapshots and find what I need. I don't have to remember which archive contains the file or manually extract several backup files to find it.

This is probably the biggest practical change for me. Backups are no longer something I regularly have to manage. They run quietly in the background, and when I actually need them, I know where to look. For a self-hosted setup, that's exactly how I want backups to work.

6 of the best open source backup options

If you're not already backing up your systems, here's where to start.

9
By  Joe Rice-Jones

My backups finally became boring

I didn't switch to Kopia because my old scripts were completely broken. I switched because I wanted to stop worrying about whether they would still work tomorrow. As my self-hosted setup grew, backups became too important to rely on a handful of scripts I had written and maintained myself.

Kopia gave me a more mature way to handle that responsibility without making my setup harder to manage. I still need to follow a sensible backup strategy and keep copies in more than one place, but I no longer feel like I'm constantly babysitting the process.

Kopia

Kopia is an open-source backup software you can self-host and point to your favorite local or cloud storage location.

item.title: DLSS has a memory cost nobody puts in the benchmarks, and 8GB card owners are paying it
item.itunes:title: DLSS has a memory cost nobody puts in the benchmarks, and 8GB card owners are paying it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If there's one thing that DLSS has taught PC gamers, it's that you can apparently have your cake and render fewer pixels too. Over the past few years, Nvidia's upscaling technology has become the go-to answer whenever a GPU starts running out of horsepower. The entire DLSS suite promises more frames while decreasing the load on the hardware, which, for 8GB graphics cards, sounds almost too good to be true.

And in one very important sense, it is. DLSS can absolutely help an 8GB GPU by reducing the memory demanded by rendering at native resolution. But the modern DLSS suite is no longer just an upscaler. Some of the features Nvidia now uses to sell its newest GPUs consume memory themselves, and on an 8GB card, there simply isn't much left to give.

Stop calling it AI slop — upscaling is democratizing high-end gaming for the 99%

Better visuals for those not on the bleeding edge.

26
By  Samarveer Singh

DLSS isn't just one feature, and your VRAM budget knows it

Some features save memory while others run up the bill

DLSS isn't really a single VRAM story. The entire suite is much more than just Super Resolution, which often becomes synonymized with Nvidia's suite. Super Resolution renders fewer pixels internally, reducing the framebuffer and render-target demands. That saving generally outweighs the reconstruction model's memory cost, which, on an 8GB GPU, is exactly the kind of help you'd want.

However, that's usually when the bill arrives. Other DLSS features enter the conversation to run up the VRAM bill, out of which Ray Reconstruction is a small spender, since it adds a transformer model to scenes bloated by ray tracing or path tracing. DLAA, on the other hand, is less subtle. It renders at full resolution, so there is no resolution saving to offset its cost. Frame Generation and Multi Frame Generation (especially 6x) are spenders, since generated frames require additional buffers.

The DLSS suite covers multiple features like Super Resolution, VSR, Frame Generation, DLAA, and Ray Reconstruction, among others.

This overhead is measured in absolute megabytes, not sympathy for your GPU. A few hundred megabytes barely registers on something like a 16GB VRAM GPU, but when all the VRAM you have is 8GB, the same allocation can consume last headroom and push the workload over the edge.

That's when data begins spilling into system RAM across PCIe, and it throws frametime spikes and stutters into the experience. DLSS may not break a GPU, but its overhead might meet a buffer that was already full.

I tested these "old" GPUs with 2026 AAA games, and the results were weirdly encouraging

Your old GPU might be more future-proof than you think

6
By  Samarveer Singh

Nvidia keeps upgrading the GPU, but not its memory

The 8GB trap has survived two generations

The RTX 4060, RTX 4060 Ti 8GB, RTX 5060 and RTX 5060 Ti 8GB aren't some ancient GPUs that are being made to put up with workloads they were never designed for. These are 8GB RTX 40- and 50-series cards, sold with the very DLSS features Nvidia uses to make its newer hardware compelling.

Moving up gets you more compute capability and more frame-generation tricks. What it doesn't get you, though, is more room for those tricks to breathe.

That's what makes a GPU like the RTX 5060 particularly funny. Multi Frame Generation is one of the headline reasons to buy into the 50-series, and yet, MFG plays a major role in adding to the memory pressure. Even if you take Frame Generation out of the equation, and simply talk about Super Resolution (DLSS 4.5) on RTX 30 series and RTX 20 series cards, the latest upscaling tech, which is inarguably the most polished, takes a much heavier memory toll on these older cards, which are exactly the ones that need Super Resolution the most.

The RTX 5060 Ti's 8GB and 16GB versions come with the same cores, same clocks, same memory bandwidth, but just by way of having more memory, the 16GB card has been measured pulling ahead by as much as 165%. When the silicon is identical, VRAM becomes the variable.

Frame generation became the baseline, and 58% of Steam gamers got left behind

Your GPU isn't obsolete, but the industry is treating it like it is

1
By  Samarveer Singh

This is where the DLSS bill comes due

Nvidia keeps selling the appetite while withholding the plate

1440p, 4K, ray tracing, path tracing, and high-resolution texture packs are exactly the workloads that consume VRAM fastest. So the DLSS suite is being marketed as the solution for demanding games while some of its most advanced features are being asked to operate inside the same 8GB ceiling those games are already threatening to breach.

It's why not every 8GB GPU owner you come across treats every DLSS toggle as free performance. Sure, upscaling remains the obvious weapon since it relieves memory pressure, but Frame Generation is more situational, and Multi Frame Generation, in particular, deserves even more scrutiny. Generating more frames doesn't make the memory holding those frames disappear, after all.

Another generation of 60-class GPUs may arrive with 8GB options next generation, all while DLSS keeps becoming more ambitious.

This isn't some hypothetical edge case confined to synthetic benchmarks, either. Texture-heavy, ray-traced workloads can already produce inconsistent frametimes on 8GB cards when memory pressure becomes the limiting factor. A counter showing three digits per second doesn't make a hitch feel any less like a hitch.

With Neural Texture Compression soon to be the next USP for RTX 60-series cards, Nvidia has the best excuse in the world to continue selling 8GB GPUs in the next couple of generations as well. And in 2026, with memory scarce and expensive, the pattern is getting harder to excuse: another generation of 60-class GPUs may very well still arrive with 8GB options while DLSS keeps becoming more ambitious. These cards will definitely be able to run the headline feature, but whether they'll have the memory to enjoy it is another question entirely.

Gigabyte GeForce RTX 5070 Ti Eagle OC Ice SFF
$660 at Amazon
DLSS is Nvidia's Achilles heel — here's why

It's great for gamers, but DLSS can only hurt Nvidia in the long run.

5
By  Ty Sherback

The memory ceiling is becoming the feature

There is a point where a specification stops being a feature and starts becoming a promise. That is where Nvidia’s 8GB cards are increasingly uncomfortable. DLSS isn't some sort of villain here, but the software ecosystem does keep expanding while the limit stays frozen. You can make an 8GB GPU smarter and faster, but you can't make eight gigabytes become twelve by giving it another acronym.

That leaves buyers with a question benchmark charts answer: how much of Nvidia’s future are you buying when the memory budget belongs to yesterday? If the answer is “most of it, provided you don’t ask too much,” then perhaps the problem was never whether DLSS works. It’s whether 8GB was ever enough for where DLSS was going.

item.title: I plugged an old laptop into my TV instead of buying another streaming box, and both got a new life
item.itunes:title: I plugged an old laptop into my TV instead of buying another streaming box, and both got a new life
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Out of all the TVs I have in my house, the oldest (and cheapest) one had reached the point where calling its software "smart" felt generous. It's an old 1080p set with a painfully dated interface, so I've spent years jumping between its built-in apps and the 2017 Fire TV Stick, depending on what I want to watch — Netflix and YouTube on TV, and Prime Video, along with all my sideloaded apps on the Fire Stick.

Then I remembered my old laptop, sitting around, useless for everything else. It was too slow to be a PC, but there was no reason it couldn't do one job. So, I plugged it into the TV, shoved it behind the screen, and started wondering whether I'd just found the better setup.

4 useful things I did with my old Fire TV Stick instead of throwing it away

There's some cool ways to repurpose a Fire TV Stick without throwing it out.

5
By  Brian Burgess

I gave my old laptop a new job

It's finally found something it was good at

The laptop I used for this experiment is not some secretly capable machine waiting for its second life. It is genuinely bad at being a computer. Ever since it received Windows 11, modern websites have been making it wheeze, and so have Google Chrome tabs, with multitasking being completely out of the question. Asking this laptop to do anything remotely demanding has been enough to remind me why it was retired in the first place.

Video streaming, however, is a much less demanding proposition. Instead of asking it to behave like a proper PC despite its aging hardware, I just needed it to output a video signal and handle a browser. That was a job it could still manage without turning every interaction into a test of my patience.

So I connected it to the TV with HDMI and simply left the cable plugged in. The laptop now lives behind the television, permanently connected and completely out of sight. I don't have to move it, open it, or treat it like a conventional computer whenever I want to watch something. The only thing I need is a remote mouse app on my phone. It gives me cursor control, scrolling, and enough control to operate everything from the sofa. With that, the laptop has become just another component of the TV, and arguably its most useful one.

HDMI 2.2 cables are here, but the hardware that needs them won't arrive for years

Infrastructure for a future that doesn't exist... yet

By  Samarveer Singh

I made Chrome look like a TV

The browser became the interface

The first thing I changed was Google Chrome's homepage. Instead of opening to a blank tab that immediately reminded me I was technically using a computer, I turned it into a TV-style launcher. Netflix, Prime Video, Jellyfin, HBO, Crunchyroll, YouTube, and the other services I use are all represented by large thumbnails that are easy to hit from the sofa.

That small change matters more than it sounds. I don't have to remember which website I need, hunt through bookmarks, or navigate a desktop full of tiny icons. I turn on the laptop, and Chrome opens by itself, and I'm looking at something that behaves much more like a streaming interface than a Windows desktop.

Google Chrome tends to use significant resources — you can use Brave or K-Meleon browser on particularly old hardware.

This is still a full web browser, with everything that implies. There just isn't a single TV operating system that could match the flexibility of Chrome. I can open an obscure streaming site, manage my Jellyfin server, watch YouTube, or just do something the TV manufacturer never supported. In fact, since I'm using Jellyfin on a web client, I also get to enjoy every single plugin I've installed on my server, which isn't something any of the native TV apps for the self-hosted media server can boast about.

It also makes the old laptop's limitations far less important. A machine that feels painfully slow with Chrome tabs, Office work, or modern Windows applications can still have plenty of life left when its entire job is decoding video and loading a handful of websites.

This useful plugin handles every Jellyfin library problem I used to fix manually

An unbelievable time saver

10
By  João Carrasqueira

The streaming box I didn't buy

Good enough isn't the same as perfect, though

There are reasons I wouldn't tell everyone to throw their streaming box in a drawer. A dedicated device wakes faster, works better with a proper remote, and is designed for someone sitting several feet away. The laptop needs considerably more cooperation. I had to set the laptop to auto-log in to the user account, then add the Chrome "kiosk" command to Task Scheduler, which launches it in fullscreen with no address bar, tabs, or UI chrome.

Despite its advantages, this system is still a computer plugged into a TV, meaning I'm dealing with more failure points than I would with a streaming stick. item.title: My 3D printer's best feature is the local camera that stops me from wasting hours on failed prints
item.itunes:title: My 3D printer's best feature is the local camera that stops me from wasting hours on failed prints
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A 3D printer can go from “that looks fine” to “why is there filament everywhere?” faster than I’d like. A corner lifts, a support snaps, or the nozzle starts dragging material around, and the printer keeps going because, as far as it knows, nothing is wrong. Remote monitoring helps, but I care more about how quickly I can get a useful look at the print than about how polished the camera interface is. For that, I’d rather have a feed that stays on my local network than depend entirely on a cloud service between me and the printer.

5 reasons to self-host your own home surveillance

Keep your recordings where they belong – with you

2
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Local video removes unnecessary steps when something starts going wrong

A printer failure can get expensive surprisingly quickly

The biggest advantage of a local camera feed is pretty mundane: there’s less in the way. The camera is on my network, the device I’m checking it from is on my network, and the video doesn’t need to go through someone else’s servers first. Many cloud feeds are responsive enough most of the time, so this isn’t about pretending they’re all terrible. I don’t see much point in adding another dependency when the printer and I are already under the same roof.

If the machine I want to look at is one room away, I shouldn’t need a working connection to a remote server to do it.

That matters most when the failure is still small. A slightly lifted edge can become a loose part, and a broken support can leave the printer laying down plastic where there’s nothing underneath it. Worse, material can start collecting around the hotend instead of on the build plate, turning a failed print into a cleanup job I really didn’t need. Seeing that after the fact is useful for figuring out what happened, but it doesn’t save the print.

I’m also more likely to check a feed when opening it doesn’t feel like a whole process. Sometimes I’m not looking for an obvious disaster at all. I’m checking whether a suspicious corner is getting worse, whether the nozzle is still laying down a clean perimeter, or whether something that looked questionable five minutes ago has settled down. Those are small decisions, but they’re often the difference between stopping a print now and wasting several more hours on it.

Local monitoring keeps working when the internet connection does not

Your home network can stay useful without internet access

Cloud monitoring has one dependency that’s easy to overlook until it gets in the way: the internet has to work. My printer, camera, computer, and phone can all be on the same network, but a cloud-first system may still stop showing me the printer because something outside my house isn’t cooperating. That has always felt backward to me. If the machine I want to look at is one room away, I shouldn’t need a working connection to a remote server to do it.

There are smaller failure points in that same setup. Cloud services have login sessions, authentication systems, app updates, maintenance windows, and server outages. Features can also move around as platforms change, which adds one more thing to troubleshoot when all I wanted was a camera view. None of that makes cloud monitoring bad. It just gives me more places to look when something simple suddenly stops working.

Long prints make that harder to shrug off. A printer running for 10, 12, or 14 hours doesn’t care whether a service is having problems or whether an app decided I needed to sign in again. It keeps printing. A local feed gives me one path to the camera that still works as long as the printer, camera, and network are up, and that starts to matter a lot more once a job stretches well past the point where I’m checking it every few minutes.

Local feeds give me control over how monitoring works

I can choose exactly where my printer video goes

Keeping the camera feed local also gives me more control over where the video goes. I can decide which devices can see it, where it’s available, and whether it ever needs to leave my network. A camera pointed at a printer isn’t exactly guarding state secrets, but I still don’t see much reason to send the feed elsewhere unless I’m getting something useful in return. Local access makes staying local the default rather than an exception.

It also means I don’t have to treat the camera as a feature that exists only within one manufacturer’s app. I can use the feed as part of whatever local setup makes sense, whether that’s a broader dashboard or something I open directly when I want to check a print. That becomes more useful once the printer stops feeling like an isolated appliance and starts acting like another device on the network. I’d rather decide how those pieces fit together than be stuck with whatever arrangement one app gives me.

There’s a practical benefit later, too. If I change cameras, printers, or monitoring software, I don’t necessarily have to rebuild everything around a different vendor’s service. The camera’s job stays the same: show me what the printer is doing. That isn’t exciting, but I’ve spent enough time tinkering with printers that I appreciate the parts of the setup that don’t demand attention.

Cloud monitoring still wins when I leave home

Remote access remains the strongest reason to use cloud

There’s one place where local-only monitoring gets less convenient very quickly: when I’m not local anymore. Once I leave home, a cloud service is appealing because the remote-access problem has already been handled for me. I open an app, sign in, pick the printer, and the feed is there. I don’t have to think about a VPN, remote network access, or any other service I’ll eventually have to remember how to configure months later.

That convenience matters when a print is going to outlast the time I’m willing to stay nearby. If I start something and then leave for dinner, run errands, or end up away from home for several hours, being able to check it from my phone is genuinely useful. Some platforms also bundle alerts and printer controls into the same interface, which makes the whole thing even easier. For many people, that’s a much better deal than setting up their own remote-access path.

And not everyone wants 3D printing to become a side networking project. There’s nothing wrong with opening the manufacturer’s app and expecting the camera to be there. That simplicity has real value, especially for someone who bought a printer to make things rather than spend an evening configuring access to it. Cloud monitoring handles that part very well.

Remote convenience does not require abandoning local monitoring

The best setup can support both kinds of access

What I don’t buy is the idea that remote convenience should require giving up direct local access. The two methods solve different problems, and there’s no reason a printer can’t support both. Local access makes sense when I’m home and on the same network. Cloud access makes sense when I’m elsewhere and need an easy way back in.

A local camera feed doesn’t have to replace remote monitoring. The most useful setup is one that lets you view the printer directly while you’re on your home network, then adds cloud or other remote access when you actually leave home.

Around the house, I’d still choose the local feed first. It gives me the shortest path to the camera and keeps outside services out of a check that doesn’t need them. When I leave, I can use whatever remote-access method makes sense, including the manufacturer’s cloud service if that’s the easiest option. I don’t need one approach to replace the other.

Cloud monitoring makes more sense to me when it’s treated as the extra layer. Notifications, remote access, and easy phone viewing are useful when I’m away. I don’t want those conveniences deciding whether I can see a printer that’s sitting down the hall. If the internet goes down for an hour, the camera beside the printer shouldn’t go with it.

Catching print failures is ultimately about shortening response time

The useful part of a camera isn’t watching a printer move for entertainment. If that were the goal, I could stand next to it. The camera matters because it lets me notice a lifted corner, a failed support, a detached part, or a growing mess before the printer spends another few hours feeding material into it. The faster and more reliably I can get that view, the more useful the camera becomes.

Cloud monitoring still has an important place when I’m away from home, and I’m not interested in giving that up. But on my own network, I don’t need the internet or somebody else’s infrastructure to see whether a print is still healthy. A local feed is easier to access, keeps working through a wider range of failures, and gives me more control over how it fits into the rest of my setup. When the printer starts doing something it shouldn’t, that’s the kind of simplicity I want.

I’m also more likely to check a feed when opening it doesn’t feel like a whole process. Sometimes I’m not looking for an obvious disaster at all. I’m checking whether a suspicious corner is getting worse, whether the nozzle is still laying down a clean perimeter, or whether something that looked questionable five minutes ago has settled down. Those are small decisions, but they’re often the difference between stopping a print now and wasting several more hours on it.

Local monitoring keeps working when the internet connection does not

Your home network can stay useful without internet access

Cloud monitoring has one dependency that’s easy to overlook until it gets in the way: the internet has to work. My printer, camera, computer, and phone can all be on the same network, but a cloud-first system may still stop showing me the printer because something outside my house isn’t cooperating. That has always felt backward to me. If the machine I want to look at is one room away, I shouldn’t need a working connection to a remote server to do it.

There are smaller failure points in that same setup. Cloud services have login sessions, authentication systems, app updates, maintenance windows, and server outages. Features can also move around as platforms change, which adds one more thing to troubleshoot when all I wanted was a camera view. None of that makes cloud monitoring bad. It just gives me more places to look when something simple suddenly stops working.

Long prints make that harder to shrug off. A printer running for 10, 12, or 14 hours doesn’t care whether a service is having problems or whether an app decided I needed to sign in again. It keeps printing. A local feed gives me one path to the camera that still works as long as the printer, camera, and network are up, and that starts to matter a lot more once a job stretches well past the point where I’m checking it every few minutes.

I can choose exactly where my printer video goes

Keeping the camera feed local also gives me more control over where the video goes. I can decide which devices can see it, where it’s available, and whether it ever needs to leave my network. A camera pointed at a printer isn’t exactly guarding state secrets, but I still don’t see much reason to send the feed elsewhere unless I’m getting something useful in return. Local access makes staying local the default rather than an exception.

It also means I don’t have to treat the camera as a feature that exists only within one manufacturer’s app. I can use the feed as part of whatever local setup makes sense, whether that’s a broader dashboard or something I open directly when I want to check a print. That becomes more useful once the printer stops feeling like an isolated appliance and starts acting like another device on the network. I’d rather decide how those pieces fit together than be stuck with whatever arrangement one app gives me.

There’s a practical benefit later, too. If I change cameras, printers, or monitoring software, I don’t necessarily have to rebuild everything around a different vendor’s service. The camera’s job stays the same: show me what the printer is doing. That isn’t exciting, but I’ve spent enough time tinkering with printers that I appreciate the parts of the setup that don’t demand attention.

Cloud monitoring still wins when I leave home

Remote access remains the strongest reason to use cloud

There’s one place where local-only monitoring gets less convenient very quickly: when I’m not local anymore. Once I leave home, a cloud service is appealing because the remote-access problem has already been handled for me. I open an app, sign in, pick the printer, and the feed is there. I don’t have to think about a VPN, remote network access, or any other service I’ll eventually have to remember how to configure months later.

That convenience matters when a print is going to outlast the time I’m willing to stay nearby. If I start something and then leave for dinner, run errands, or end up away from home for several hours, being able to check it from my phone is genuinely useful. Some platforms also bundle alerts and printer controls into the same interface, which makes the whole thing even easier. For many people, that’s a much better deal than setting up their own remote-access path.

And not everyone wants 3D printing to become a side networking project. There’s nothing wrong with opening the manufacturer’s app and expecting the camera to be there. That simplicity has real value, especially for someone who bought a printer to make things rather than spend an evening configuring access to it. Cloud monitoring handles that part very well.

Remote convenience does not require abandoning local monitoring

The best setup can support both kinds of access

What I don’t buy is the idea that remote convenience should require giving up direct local access. The two methods solve different problems, and there’s no reason a printer can’t support both. Local access makes sense when I’m home and on the same network. Cloud access makes sense when I’m elsewhere and need an easy way back in.

A local camera feed doesn’t have to replace remote monitoring. The most useful setup is one that lets you view the printer directly while you’re on your home network, then adds cloud or other remote access when you actually leave home.

Around the house, I’d still choose the local feed first. It gives me the shortest path to the camera and keeps outside services out of a check that doesn’t need them. When I leave, I can use whatever remote-access method makes sense, including the manufacturer’s cloud service if that’s the easiest option. I don’t need one approach to replace the other.

Cloud monitoring makes more sense to me when it’s treated as the extra layer. Notifications, remote access, and easy phone viewing are useful when I’m away. I don’t want those conveniences deciding whether I can see a printer that’s sitting down the hall. If the internet goes down for an hour, the camera beside the printer shouldn’t go with it.

Catching print failures is ultimately about shortening response time

The useful part of a camera isn’t watching a printer move for entertainment. If that were the goal, I could stand next to it. The camera matters because it lets me notice a lifted corner, a failed support, a detached part, or a growing mess before the printer spends another few hours feeding material into it. The faster and more reliably I can get that view, the more useful the camera becomes.

Cloud monitoring still has an important place when I’m away from home, and I’m not interested in giving that up. But on my own network, I don’t need the internet or somebody else’s infrastructure to see whether a print is still healthy. A local feed is easier to access, keeps working through a wider range of failures, and gives me more control over how it fits into the rest of my setup. When the printer starts doing something it shouldn’t, that’s the kind of simplicity I want.

item.title: I stopped trusting online PDF tools after finding out what one Docker container does offline
item.itunes:title: I stopped trusting online PDF tools after finding out what one Docker container does offline
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
PDFs are an unpleasant fact of life. They're a pain to work with and edit, and yet nearly every important document you'll ever sign will appear as a PDF. Do you really trust those free editing websites to safeguard your information?

Here's the thing: I don't want to upload a document containing my address, banking info, Social Security number, or any other vital piece of information to a random website, no matter how convenient it might be. If you find yourself needing to edit a PDF, you can self-host a tool like Stirling PDF that will do the job far better than one of those sketchy sites, and it does all of it locally.

I don't upload sensitive PDFs anymore

Sensitive files stay on my machine

As a freelancer, I deal with a lot of tax forms. These forms all, inevitably, have to be sent back as a PDF, which means I need a PDF editor to fill them out. At the start of my career, I'd use less-than-reputable PDF editing sites out of convenience. Later, I used tools like Photoshop to edit. Yes, Acrobat would have been a better choice, but I didn't know at that time. It's a miracle I didn't experience identity theft after revealing all that personal information on those forms, but I somehow made it through.

With Stirling PDF, I don't take that chance. Everything happens on my device. I can easily edit a 1040 tax form and enter my Social Security number, name, and address, or enter my banking info for direct deposit, without worrying that I'm giving a bad actor a direct line to my funds.

That's not to say that online PDF editors are necessarily unsafe. I don't know whether they are or not (although anything I can't verify myself will get the side eye until I can). My reasoning is more along the lines of: why take the risk if I don't have to?

I tried a dozen free PDF editors and finally found the best one

From splitting and merging to OCR, this one's got it all

17
By  Sumukh Rao

A single Docker container replaces a host of utilities

Anything those sites can do, Stirling PDF can do better

Here's the thing about random PDF editors on the web: they're usually limited in what they can do. Stirling PDF, on the other hand, is a fully-featured suite that can handle nearly anything you throw at it. Text editing is an obvious use, of course, but you can also use it to merge PDFs, compress files, scan the text with OCR (optical character recognition), and convert file types. If that's not enough, you can also sign and timestamp a PDF.

It doesn't stop there. If you have a password-protected PDF and you want to make it easier to access, you can do that (provided you know the password). Stirling PDF doesn't act as a cracker, however, so if you have forgotten the password, you'll need a different tool.

It also has tools for cropping, splitting, and rotating pages, adjusting the scale and size, and much more. In other words, if there's something you need to do to a PDF form, Stirling PDF can probably handle it without issue.

It works even offline

And that gives me peace of mind

Using those online tools requires, well, an internet connection. And while it's not often that I'm entirely offline in 2026, I appreciate the fact that Stirling PDF works without the need for the web.

Well, after setup, that is.

Once the files are downloaded and the Docker container is up and running, I can access Stirling PDF with or without Wi-Fi. The documents are processed locally, not on a remote server, so it makes no difference whether I have access to the web or not.

The fact that it works without internet is a pretty good indicator that everything is processed on-device, rather than on a remote server somewhere, and that gives me peace of mind when working with sensitive personal data.

I replaced Adobe Acrobat with Stirling PDF, but the real cost wasn't what I expected

The switch I never officially made.

By  Shekhar Vaidya

But Stirling PDF isn't necessarily easier than using a website

You still need to install it and set it up

Stirling PDF impresses me in many ways, but I won't pretend it's necessarily easy to use. I'm familiar with self-hosting, so installing a Docker container wasn't a problem, but I remember the first time I fired up Docker and started reading the documentation. It was overwhelming, and I completely understand why self-hosting can be intimidating for users who aren't as tech-savvy.

An online tool is simple to use. You just upload the file, make your changes, and download it again. To use Stirling PDF, you need to install Docker, pull the image, handle the ports, and then create an account, and that's all before you start working on the PDF itself.

Case in point: the default installation didn't work for me, as Stirling PDF's default port was already in use by something else. I had to change the configured port number before I could use it.

That's a lot of effort if you don't work with PDFs that often, but in my opinion, the privacy is worth it.

Stirling PDF is possibly the best PDF tool I've ever used

I've worked as a freelancer for 15 years at this point, and that means I've dealt with a lot of forms and, in turn, a lot of PDF utilities. Stirling PDF might be the best of them all, and I don't say that lightly. Acrobat is a good application, but the cost is too steep, especially when Stirling PDF can do everything I need, and the only cost is a bit of my time.

Stirling PDF

Stirling is a privacy-first, open-source PDF platform that combines everyday editing tools with scalable AI automation, APIs, and self-hosted deployment options.

item.title: My NAS has been running 24/7 for 15 years, but Docker finally gave it a reason to stay on
item.itunes:title: My NAS has been running 24/7 for 15 years, but Docker finally gave it a reason to stay on
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been on the NAS bandwagon for almost fifteen years. What started off as an easy way to back up my files has quickly turned into a storage obsession. But not just that. Over the years, my NAS has become what I use for a whole range of services that I want around my home.

From home automation to wireless scanning and dashboards, my NAS powers all these services, and Docker is what makes this possible. As good as Synology's operating system is, it has limits on the kinds of applications it supports. Even for apps Synology supports, I prefer to run them in their own containers rather than install them on the operating system, keeping configuration and data segregated. Put together, it gives me a much cleaner way to add services to my home setup.

5 ways to turn a NAS into the heart of your smart home

Centralize your storage and your smart home.

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Home Assistant made my NAS more than a storage server

An always-on home for all my self-hosted services

Home Assistant is perhaps the biggest example of why I use Docker since it's where my self-hosting journey began. I need my home automation system to stay powered on all the time. That automatically makes a NAS the perfect fit. The system stays powered on and connected to my network. If I've already got a computer running 24/7, there's little reason to spin up another machine. Moreover, I'm certainly not complaining that NAS drives are designed to be power efficient. For a device that's constantly powered on, any power savings are a good move.

Home Assistant on my NAS has also grown well beyond just another way to turn lights on or off. I use it as the central control point for a growing number of devices and automations around my home. Having everything running from the NAS means I don't have to think if the server is on or off. Just as important is the fact that, given the appliance-like format, I don't have to hide away my NAS. It looks great just sitting on a desk or shelf.

Circling back to Docker, though, using containers for running your software comes with certain advantages. I can keep Home Assistant segregated from the rest of the NAS, and the same goes for the wide range of experimental services I end up running. The application has its own container, while configuration and data sit in the storage that I've allocated for it. Anytime I restart, update, or recreate the container, it doesn't affect the other services running on the machine. That's important on a machine as critical as the one powering all your self-hosted services.

This same idea extends to every other self-hosted service I run on my NAS. After all, a music server is no good if it isn't easy to access. A NAS that is designed to be always-on is the perfect host.

Docker allows me to experiment beyond Synology's software ecosystem

Running services that Synology doesn't offer

  • Credit:  
  • Credit: 
  • Credit:  
  • Credit: 

Another big reason Docker has completely changed how I use my NAS is that it lets me run services Synology doesn't offer. In the early days of my self-hosting journey, I used to get annoyed by the limited scope of services and tools available as a package via Synology. With Docker, I can run practically any service without being limited to the software available via Synology's ecosystem.

Take my wireless scanning setup, for example. I run Scanservjs in a container to turn my scanner into a network service that I can access from my computers without having to connect my scanner directly to them. Using Docker on my NAS let me set this up with no hassle at all.

Similarly, I use Homebridge to connect and expose devices and services around my home. Homebridge is, in my opinion, one of the flakiest home automation tools and one that needs careful handling. Since it runs as a Docker container, I can update, roll back, or restart without touching anything else on my home server.

Using Docker has opened up a world of services on my NAS that I probably wouldn't have used otherwise. Just the other day, I deployed a keyboard-based dashboard that lets me launch any of my self-hosted services with two to three keystrokes at most. Over the weekend, I tried out a music recommendation engine.

Docker gives me a low-friction way to try out new software without worrying about the consequences of installing experimental services on my NAS. If I find a self-hosted application that looks useful, I don't have to make a permanent change to the NAS operating system. I can deploy it as a container, give it the storage it needs, and remove it later if I don't think I'll use it much.

Docker turned my NAS into a self-hosting platform

Docker isn't the reason I have a NAS, but it has made my NAS much more useful than it used to be. The storage continues to be the foundation, while containers let me build a stack of services on top of it. The result is a NAS that does much more than hold my files. In fact, thanks to Docker, it has become a critical part of my self-hosted infrastructure.

Docker

Docker Desktop is a one-click-install application for your Mac, Linux, or Windows environment that lets you build, share, and run containerized applications and microservices. It provides a straightforward GUI (Graphical User Interface) that lets you manage your containers, applications, and images directly from your machine.
Docker Desktop reduces the time spent on complex setups so you can focus on writing code. It takes care of port mappings, file system concerns, and other default settings, and is regularly updated with bug fixes and security updates.

AMD's Ryzen CPUs have transformed the company's prospects, from an also-ran running out of money quickly, to the class leader in desktop and server processors. Recent releases like the Ryzen 9000 series have cemented its place ahead of rival Intel, and it doesn't look like that will change any time soon. With that knowledge, you might be tempted to use AMD for your CPU next build, and that's a good idea, but you should also know what little foibles you're getting.

The biggest bugbear that AMD has tried to throw off is RAM compatibility. Part of this is because of Ryzen's architecture, with chiplets connected by the Infinity Fabric, an interconnect that passes data between the chiplets and the RAM. It's also partly because when Ryzen first came out, Intel was the dominant factor, so early CPUs had to use RAM modules that were tweaked for Intel CPUs, and didn't always run well with AMD. With Ryzen-specific modules on the market, that's also changed, but even with that, you should know about some potential issues and how to get past them.

Infinity Fabric clock ratio issues

There's a golden ratio for Ryzen and it's not 1:1.618

While many of these tips could apply to other CPUs, the Infinity Fabric is Ryzen specific. Essentially, it connects AMD's CPU chiplets to each other, but also acts as a chiplet-chiplet, CPU-CPU, and CPU-GPU interconnect for all data transfer on the motherboard. The Infinity Fabric runs at a specific frequency, FCLK, connecting all the parts of the CPU together. This can be linked to the memory clock or unlinked with a series of dividers and multipliers, so you can run higher memory than the memory controller officially supports.

There are also two other clocks in Ryzen's memory architecture:

  • UCLK (Unified Memory Controller Clock): controls the speed of the memory controller in the I/O die
  • MCLK (Memory Clock): corresponds to the speed of the memory modules

This gives a FLCK:ULCK:MCLK ratio that's used across all generations of Ryzen, but in a slightly different way.

For Ryzen up to and including 5000 series, AMD recommends a 1:1:1 ratio, but FCLK can be tweaked for better performance. Verify in BIOS that the UCLK ratio is set to 1:1 with MCLK, which will be half the rate of your memory speed. On Ryzen 7000 and 9000, AMD recommends an Auto:1:1 ratio, so the only factor that changes is UCLK, which will run at half the speed of the memory controller once you get to a certain point.

For AM4 Ryzen processors, the 1:1 ratio is maintained up to DDR4-3600 (5000 series can do DDR4-3733)

For AM5 Ryzen processors, the 1:1 ratio is maintained up to DDR5-6000 (Ryzen 9000 can do DDR5-6400)

The problem with this is that once you unlink the two, you get a performance hit. This can be okay, as if your RAM is fast enough, the latency hit is overcome. For AM4, DDR4-4000 was enough to overcome the latency when I was using that, but it was a pain to get working so DDR4-3600 is still the best option. For AM5, if you can get 8,000MT/s running on your CPU, that will be slightly better than 6,000 1:1, but not really by that much.

Mixed memory brands and modules

This is never a great idea but it's even worse on Ryzen

It's 2025, and mixing RAM kits can still be a risky proposition. It's tricky enough on Intel where the memory controller is usually better, but with Ryzen it can be a non-starter right out of the gate. It doesn't have to be from different manufacturers either, just the differences from two production runs of the same SKU can cause issues. These could include lowered speeds, lowered capacity, or random crashes and BSODs, so it's a tricky choice.

You might be able to get away with mixed kits if you match the following exactly:

  • Memory type (DDR4 with DDR4, DDR5 with DDR5)
  • Speed (MHz)
  • CAS latency timings
  • Voltage requirements
  • Capacity per module

Even then, Ryzen's memory controller is known to be sensitive, and they might not work. The only way to really be sure is to buy a matched kit, whether that's for two DIMMs, four DIMMs, or eight DIMMs if you're buying for a Threadripper motherboard. Oh, and if you're filling all the RAM slots you need to know that you might not get the rated speed, because the memory controller on Ryzen 1000, 2000, 3000, and 5000 series slows right down if you do. On AM5 motherboards you might also run the risk of slower speeds, but it's less of a consideration.

Conflicts between single and dual rank modules

Just like brands and speeds, this can have your system crashing out

I will split this one into two sections, because AM4 Ryzen CPUs have issues with single and dual-rank DIMMs, while AM5 Ryzen only has the usual issues that any CPU would. The general rule of thumb is never to mix single-rank and dual-rank in the same memory channel. You can get away with using mixed modules if they're in different memory channels, and you have to disable memory interleaving in your BIOS to do so.

DDR4 with 8GB capacity is single-rank (usually), while anything higher will be dual-rank. That's the easiest way to guess if it doesn't say on the product page. For DDR5, 24GB is the cut-off where single-rank ends, and anything higher will be dual-rank.

Ryzen for the AM5 socket, however, uses DDR5, and while the memory controller might not be rated for super speeds, those speeds don't change if you're using single- or dual-rank DIMMs.

EXPO or XMP issues

While XMP and EXPO aren't completely different technologies, they're not always comparable. XMP was a standard developed by Intel, while DOCP or EXPO are standards developed by AMD. They might define very similar profiles, but your motherboard might treat those very differently. That said, neither is a guaranteed overclock on any system, Intel or Ryzen, but you can do a few things to ensure the least amount of disappointment.

For Ryzen, checking the QVL for your motherboard is one of the things you should do before buying anything. If the kit you've been eyeing isn't on that list, or is of a higher MT/s than those kits, you can still buy it but know you're probably not going to get the best out of it. Increasing VRAM voltage by 0.05V from the rated specification can give you enough of a boost to get the rated speeds.

Voltage and memory controller limitations

Each generation of Ryzen comes with different considerations

Every generation of Ryzen has a slightly different memory controller with varying capabilities and requirements to run at their best. The newer the Ryzen CPU the better, and AM5 Ryzen chips are easy to run at higher speeds if you have the right motherboard. Remember it's not just the CPU that governs RAM max speeds, so pair with a premium motherboard for the best chance of higher MT/s.

These general rules will help you choose RAM that fits your CPU:

  • Ryzen 1000/2000: Struggle beyond DDR4-3200, weak memory controllers
  • Ryzen 3000/5000: Good up to DDR4-3600 with proper tuning
  • Ryzen 7000+: Native DDR5 support, aim for DDR5-5600 to DDR5-6000 at CL30 or below

Other things to monitor are SoC voltage, which should be under 1.2V for safety no matter which generation of Ryzen you own. DDR4 can easily run up to 1.5V for daily use (I ran mine at this for two years before upgrading to AM5 with DDR5), and DDR5 can vary between 1.1-1.35V depending on the speed you are running at. I wouldn't be too worried about RAM voltage. In my years of computing, the number of truly dead RAM kits I've had is small, and those were faulty, not abused with voltage.

Ryzen has had its share of RAM issues, but they're mostly ironed out now

Look, I don't want to put you off buying one of the best CPUs around. AMD's Ryzen are the class leader in most segments, and if you go Intel you have other issues to contend with. Buying RAM for Ryzen isn't that difficult, you just need to go into it armed with the right information and tempered expectations. Then you'll be fine, whatever you choose.

EXPO or XMP issues

While Ryzen motherboards can read XMP values they might not always work

While XMP and EXPO aren't completely different technologies, they're not always comparable. XMP was a standard developed by Intel, while DOCP or EXPO are standards developed by AMD. They might define very similar profiles, but your motherboard might treat those very differently. That said, neither is a guaranteed overclock on any system, Intel or Ryzen, but you can do a few things to ensure the least amount of disappointment.

For Ryzen, checking the QVL for your motherboard is one of the things you should do before buying anything. If the kit you've been eyeing isn't on that list, or is of a higher MT/s than those kits, you can still buy it but know you're probably not going to get the best out of it. Voltage and memory controller limitations

Each generation of Ryzen comes with different considerations

Every generation of Ryzen has a slightly different memory controller with varying capabilities and requirements to run at their best. The newer the Ryzen CPU the better, and AM5 Ryzen chips are easy to run at higher speeds if you have the right motherboard. Remember it's not just the CPU that governs RAM max speeds, so pair with a premium motherboard for the best chance of higher MT/s.

  • Ryzen 1000/2000: Struggle beyond DDR4-3200, weak memory controllers
  • Ryzen 3000/5000: Good up to DDR4-3600 with proper tuning
  • Ryzen 7000+: Native DDR5 support, aim for DDR5-5600 to DDR5-6000 at CL30 or below

I wouldn't be too worried about RAM voltage. In my years of computing, the number of truly dead RAM kits I've had is small, and those were faulty, not abused with voltage.

Look, I don't want to put you off buying one of the best CPUs around. AMD's Ryzen are the class leader in most segments, and if you go Intel you have other issues to contend with. Buying RAM for Ryzen isn't that difficult, you just need to go into it armed with the right information and tempered expectations. Then you'll be fine, whatever you choose.

item.title: The Aurzen ZIP Pro folding projector brings native 1080p video anywhere
item.itunes:title: The Aurzen ZIP Pro folding projector brings native 1080p video anywhere
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Portable projectors have always involved a compromise. Make one small enough to carry, and you usually lose brightness, resolution, or battery life along the way. Make one bright and sharp enough to look good on a wall, and you get too much bulk to bring it anywhere beyond the living room. Aurzen's new ZIP Pro attempts to close that gap, packing native 1080p resolution into a tri-fold body that shrinks down small enough to fit in a jacket pocket.

Aurzen calls it the world's first tri-fold Full HD pocket projector, which builds directly on the original ZIP, the company's earlier tri-fold projector that topped out at 720p. The ZIP Pro keeps the same folding Z-shape design that made the original easy to set up almost anywhere, while pushing the resolution, brightness, and feature set further for those wanting something closer to a proper home cinema experience anywhere.

The Aurzen ZIP Pro is a tri-fold pocket projector delivering native 1080p resolution in a body that folds down to jacket-pocket size. A 10.7mm optical engine provides 200 ANSI lumens of brightness, while the Z-shape folding design doubles as a built-in stand. Connect wirelessly via AirPlay, Miracast, Google Cast, or AirLink P2P, or wire in over USB-C. Its 38Wh battery also offers up to 2.5 hours of viewing per charge.

See at Aurzen

The Aurzen ZIP Pro’s defining feature is its tri-fold construction. The body splits into three hinged sections that open into a Z-shape, which also acts as a built-in multi-angle stand. That means there is no separate tripod or mount to carry or lose. You unfold the device, angle it toward a wall or ceiling, and it holds itself in place.

Folded, ZIP Pro measures 115mm by 97mm by 44mm and weighs 586g, with a total volume of 487cc. It is noticeably larger and heavier than the original ZIP, which folds down to 84mm by 78mm by 26mm and weighs just 280g, though the increase in size tracks with what has been added inside. Aurzen says the extra bulk is necessary to accommodate a brighter light source, a bigger battery and a proper full HD panel.

Setup is meant to be quick rather than fiddly. ZIP Pro uses Time-of-Flight autofocus alongside four-point keystone correction, so the projector can sharpen and square off the image automatically once it is aimed at a surface, instead of manually adjusting focus and geometry every time it is moved.

Full HD resolution from a slim optical engine

Credit: Aurzen

Where the original ZIP topped out at 720p, ZIP Pro moves up to native 1080p resolution at 60Hz, delivered through what Aurzen describes as a 10.7mm ultra-slim optical engine. Brightness is rated at 200 ANSI lumens in its Conference mode, dropping to 150 lumens in Normal mode and 100 lumens in ECO mode to help preserve battery life.

Those figures put ZIP Pro firmly in the category of projectors designed for dim or dark rooms rather than daylight viewing. Aurzen's own materials describe a viewing size of 60 to 80 inches in dark environments, and with a contrast ratio of 300:1 and color gamut of 85% NTSC, this is a device best suited to evening films, gaming sessions, or shows in a bedroom or hotel room rather than a bright living room with the curtains open.

Throw ratio sits at 1.2, with a supported projection distance of 0.5m to 3m, so there is some flexibility in how far back the projector needs to sit from the wall.

Connecting without cables, or with them

Credit: Aurzen

The ZIP Pro supports a wide range of ways to get content onto the screen. For wireless mirroring, it works with AirPlay, Miracast, DLNA and Google Cast, covering most phones, tablets and laptops without extra apps. Aurzen has also built in its own AirLink P2P mirroring, which the company says allows a direct wireless connection between a device and the projector without a Wi-Fi network to route through. That could be useful in hotel rooms or outdoor settings where a shared network is not available.

For a wired connection, the ZIP Pro uses USB-C with DP Alt Mode, letting it take a direct video signal from compatible phones and laptops. Aurzen also highlights an industry-first direct Type-C projection setup for the Nintendo Switch, paired with a dedicated Game Mode intended to reduce input lag for a more responsive picture during play.

Audio built for shared and private viewing

Credit: Aurzen

Sound comes from a pair of 2W stereo speakers built into the unit, alongside a headphone-style option for those looking to keep the audio to themselves. The ZIP Pro supports dual Bluetooth headphone output, which Aurzen describes as an industry first, allowing two sets of Bluetooth headphones to connect and play audio at the same time. In practice, that means two people could watch the same film side by side, each listening through their own headphones, without disturbing anyone nearby. Noise from the projector itself is rated at 24dB in ECO mode, rising to 28dB in Normal mode and 35dB in Conference mode.

For anyone watching mobile-first content, a Vertical Full-Screen Mode is designed to fill the display with vertical video without leaving black bars on each side, which suits short-form video shot for phone screens.

Battery life and charging

The projector has a built-in 38Wh battery, made up of two 5,000mAh cells, which powers the ZIP Pro for up to 2.5 hours of viewing in ECO mode. That compares with roughly 1.5 hours from the original ZIP, reflecting the larger battery Aurzen has fitted alongside the brighter light source. Charging is handled over USB-C with support for 65W PD fast charging, and the projector can also draw power from a portable power bank, which makes it easy to use while traveling or when you’re in places without easy access to a wall outlet.

A touch display for status at a glance

Credit: Aurzen

Rather than relying purely on physical buttons, the ZIP Pro has what Aurzen calls a Smart Touch Display on its body. It shows battery level and connection status and offers virtual controls, along with a customizable splash screen. This is a small addition, but one that means checking on charge level or connection status does not require turning to a phone or squinting at a status light.

Who will love the ZIP Pro

Aurzen positions ZIP Pro for business travelers, people who want a bedroom entertainment setup without a permanently mounted TV, outdoor users who want a brighter and more capable device than the original ZIP, and anyone hosting games in a dedicated room. That sits alongside the original ZIP, which is focused on lightweight outdoor use, casual setups, and creative or DIY projects where absolute portability matters more than resolution.

Put simply, if the standard ZIP was about making projection as easy and portable as possible, the ZIP Pro is about keeping that same folding convenience while closing the gap with a proper home projector in terms of resolution, brightness, and battery life. Whether that trade-off of slightly more size and weight for a sharper, longer-lasting picture makes sense will depend on how you plan to use it. For those who found the original ZIP appealing yet wanted a sharper image, ZIP Pro looks like a fairly direct answer.

The ZIP Pro is available for pre-order now on Aurzen's website.

Brought to you by Aurzen.
